claims.claim: D. pulex's growth rate 'decreased dramatically between 1.5 and 1 mg Ca L⁻¹', warm water and low food raising the threshold to 1.5 mg/L (Ashforth & Yan 2008; abstract only)
claims.location: p. 420 (PDF p. 1), Abstract (read on the page image); Results, p. 425 (PDF p. 6), r and the second reproductive threshold
claims.quote: the intrinsic rate of natural increase, r, decreased dramatically between 1.5 and 1 mg
claims.conditions: laboratory, one clone of D. pulex in a fully defined medium; Ca 0.1, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 5, 10 mg/L × high food (30 µg Chl a/L) and low food (3 µg Chl a/L) × 20, 24, 28, 32 °C; 15-day experiment. Survival threshold 0.1–0.5 mg Ca/L regardless of temperature or food; at 32 °C no reproduction
claims.note: Confirmed, with two wording points: (1) the 'growth rate' is the population's intrinsic rate of increase r, not body growth — say 'population growth rate (r)'; (2) the paper now has the full text, so '(abstract only)' can go. 'Higher temperatures and reduced algal biomass … raising the reproductive threshold to 1.5 mg Ca L-1' is in the abstract; the results describe it as a second reproductive threshold between 1 and 1.5 mg/L at warmer temperatures and low algal density (delayed maturity, fewer and smaller broods below 1.5 mg/L). At high food r fell significantly at all temperatures from 1.5 to 1 mg/L.

notes: The authors' conclusion: fresh waters need at least 0.5 mg Ca/L to sustain D. pulex, and as much as 1.5 mg/L under concurrent lower algal biomass and warmer water. Against Hot Brook's analog median of ~2.0 mg Ca/L (paper §3.3.7) this supports the paper's 'probably not controlling'. The warm treatments (24–28 °C) are near Hot Brook's summer surface maximum.
